power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.121", Sentence = "Post-hoc comparisons revealed that S. aureus had significantly higher 155 contamination levels compared to total coliforms (mean difference=1.321 log CFU/mL, p<0.001) and 156 thermotolerant coliforms (mean difference=0.462 log CFU/mL, p=0.121, not significant)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Bacteriological surface contamination is a key pathway for pathogen transmission, with potential implications for microbial exposure.
Shared bicycles at Makerere University provide sustainable transport, but frequent handling of handlebars may facilitate colonization and spread of bacteria such as E. coli.

This study aimed to identify prevalent bacterial species on shared bicycle handlebars, their microbial load and antimicrobial profiles, and users' hand hygiene practices influencing contamination at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda.
Methods: We randomly sampled 100 shared bicycles and interviewed their respective users.
Handlebar swabs were cultured and analyzed by culture-based enumeration.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using disk diffusion across six antibiotics.
Hand hygiene data were collected using structured questionnaire guides.

Descriptive statistics summarized bacterial counts, F-tests assessed statistical differences within and across bacterial species, and modified poisson regression examined associations between hygiene practices and contamination.
Results: Contamination was detected on 56% (56/100) of the sampled handlebars.
From the 56 contaminated samples, 13 contained more than one bacterial species and 75 isolates were recovered, with S. aureus at 68% (51/75) as the most prevalent isolate.
Microbial loads differed significantly across species (F (2, 63) = 12.78, p < 0.0001). 35 of the 75 isolates yielded bacteriological growth and were subjected to AST.

text.text: Most isolates were resistant to erythromycin at 71% (25/35), and S. aureus showed resistance to five of six antibiotics, indicating multidrug resistance.
Users who did not clean their hands were (APR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.11-1.98) 1.6 times more likely to contaminate handlebars.
Conclusion: Shared bicycle handlebars at Makerere University were contaminated with potentially pathogenic bacteria, indicating a potential hygiene concern.

text.text: These findings highlight the risk of crosscontamination during cash transactions in shared mobility systems.
Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, adopted the bicycle sharing program in 2023 to facilitate mobility of the staff, students, and visitors around the 350-acre campus.

Makerere University, with an estimated population of 40,000 individuals, operates approximately 120 shared bicycles, yielding a user-to-bicycle ratio of 1:300, underscoring handlebars as frequently touched surfaces.
The initiative supports sustainable mobility but also raises public health concerns, as frequent handlebar handling combined with cash payments increases the potential for microbial exposure.
Therefore, this study aimed to understand the extent of bacteriological contamination on the handlebars and hand hygiene practices of the shared bicycle users at Makerere University, Kampala, Uganda.
This cross-sectional study was conducted at Makerere University, a public institution in Kampala, Uganda, between June and August 2025 using quantitative data collection methods.

The sustainable mobility program at Makerere University has twelve docking stations, but only eight were actively functional, with bicycles used by students, staff, and visitors at the time of data collection.
Makerere University was selected because it is the only institution with a bicycle-sharing program, offering a unique context for study.

Shared bicycles were chosen over other public means of transport like taxis and motorcycles since the user holds the handlebars, which involves repeated hand contact by multiple users, making them particularly susceptible to microbial contamination.
This study was carried out among bicycle users and shared bicycles at Makerere University.
Eligible participants were students, staff, and visitors who were actively using the shared bicycles during the study period and consented to provide hand hygiene information.
Only shared bicycles in routine circulation and accessible at docking stations were included for sampling.
The study used 100 shared-bicycle users and their corresponding ridden bicycles.
At docking stations, multiple users often retrieved bicycles concurrently.
Swab collection from the bicycle handlebars and interviews were conducted on one participant at a time whose trip had ended.
The users were present, and recruitment was contingent on participant consent, while individuals who declined were not included in the study.
The Kish and Leslie (1965) (14) formula was used.

Considering a Z-score (95% confidence interval) of 1.96, the prevalence of contamination of bicycle handlebars with bacteria of 50%, and a degree of error of 5%, 384 participant/bicycles will be studied.
We adjusted for a finite population of 120 shared bicycles using Cochran's (1977) formula, generating a total of 92.
The minimum required sample size after finite population correction was 92.
However, laboratory analysis was conducted on a rolling basis, and some collected samples did not yield bacterial growth.
To compensate for these losses and ensure sufficient analyzable data, we modestly increased recruitment to 100 participants, increasing the number of observations available for analysis of the study.
Surface swab samples were collected from bicycle handlebars and transported to the Microbiology Diagnostic Laboratory (Biosafety level-2) in Makerere University for analysis.
Subsequently, a structured questionnaire was used to collect data on the bicycle users' hand hygiene practices.
Each bicycle and the respective user were both assigned identical study identification numbers to enable merging of questionnaire responses and the bacteriological profiles found on the bicycle.
Handlebar swab samples were collected with sterile, wet cotton swabs of 15mm (15).
text.formatted: Handlebar swab samples were collected with sterile, wet cotton swabs of 15mm <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: The ends of the swabs were aseptically broken to fit in a Falcon tube (Conda Lab, Spain) of 15ml capacity with a screw cap and conical bottom containing 5ml of Stuart's transport medium (Hi Media Laboratories Limited, India).
They were placed in a cooler box and then transported to the laboratory for analysis.
In the laboratory, the swabs were removed from the Falcon tube using sterile forceps and placed in a standard test tube of 20mL containing 9mL of sterile peptone water (Conda Lab Madrid, Spain).
The primary bacteriological suspension was labelled 10 -1 and agitated for about 30 seconds using a pipette tip to extract bacteria from the swab.
This was followed by a 10-fold serial dilution to get 10 -2 and 10 - 3 solutions.

These were separately inoculated and surface-spread onto sterile Mannitol Salt Agar plates (MSA) and MacConkey Agar plates (MAC), both manufactured by Hardy Diagnostics in Santa Maria, U.S.A. The plates were placed in an incubator (Memmert, Germany) at 37 °C for MSA and 45 °C for MAC for about 20 hours.
Microbial load was then calculated as CFU=N/df x V, where N=number of colonies, df=dilution factor (10 -3 ), V=volume plated (10 -1 ), and expressed as log CFU/mL× 10².
Subculturing was done to obtain pure colonies of the isolates (Muhumuza et al., 2018).

The presumptive bacteriological pure colonies identified by their morphology and color that is pink for coliforms and yellow for S. aureus were then subjected to standard biochemical tests for confirmation (17, 18).

text.text: Subculturing was done to obtain pure cultures of the isolates, from which discrete colonies were emulsified into a test tube with 1 mL of normal saline.
The bacteriological suspension was compared to a standard of 0.5 McFarland to compare the optical density.
If the turbidity matched, then a sterile cotton swab was immersed in the suspension and used to inoculate Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA) plates by surface spreading.
Antibiotic disks (Hardy Diagnostics, U.S.A) were applied to the MHA plates using sterile forceps.

The choice of antibiotics was obtained from Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (22), these were Amoxicillin-clavulanic (AMC32 µg), Gentamicin (CN120 µg), Ciprofloxacin (CIP5 µg), Cefoxitin (FOX30 µg), Imipenem (IPM10 µg), Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim (SXT25 µg), Erythromycin (E15 µg), and Tetracycline (Te30 µg).

Users' hand hygiene data were obtained using structured questionnaires administered to the participants electronically with Kobo Collect.
The questionnaire was developed from literature on hand hygiene and microbial contamination (23, 24).
text.formatted: The questionnaire was developed from literature on hand hygiene and microbial contamination <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24)</ref>.

text.text: The tool was structured into four sections on demographics, bicycle usage patterns, hygiene practices, and additional information on contamination perceptions.
The questionnaire guide was refined through expert input by supervisors and pre-testing.
The pre-testing of the tool was carried out amongst 9 classmates that are shared bicycle users at Makerere University to assess the relevance, clarity, and suitability of the questions.
Feedback obtained during the pre-test was used to refine the questionnaire before the main data collection.
The classmates who participated in the pre-test were excluded from the final study sample.
Trained research assistants administered the interviews face-to-face at docking stations, approaching users immediately after parking their bicycles to capture real-time responses.
Data were analyzed using STATA software version 18.

Descriptive statistics was used to summarize the socio-demographic characteristics of participants and to present the distribution of hand hygiene practices and levels of bacteriological contamination observed on bicycle handlebars.
One-way ANOVA with F-tests was used to compare mean microbial loads across bacterial species, to determine whether contamination intensity differed significantly between isolates.
In contrast, chi-square tests were applied to assess associations between categorical predictors e.g., hand hygiene practices, age group, frequency of bicycle use and contamination status.

Modified poisson regression was used to estimate the prevalence ratios and their 95% confidence intervals to quantify associations between bacteriological contamination and hand hygiene practices while adjusting for potential confounders (e.g., age, sex, frequency of bicycle use, college affiliation, and access to hygiene facilities).
Ethical approval was obtained from the Makerere University School of Public Health Higher Degrees Committee, and the study protocol number with MakSPH-REC was 599.

Permission was granted by Makerere University administration and the shared bicycle service provider to conduct the study formally within institutional guidelines and with the cooperation of the service operators.
Written informed consent was obtained from all study participants before bicycle handlebar sampling and questionnaire administration.
Confidentiality and anonymity were strictly maintained throughout the study.
Anonymity was ensured by assigning unique codes to participants instead of recording personal identifiers such as names or contact details.
All responses were stored in password-protected files on the principal investigator's computer, accessible only to the research team.
Data were used solely for research purposes and reported in aggregate form, preventing identification of individual participants.

Biosafety protocols were rigorously observed during sample collection and laboratory analysis, including the use of personal protective equipment, sterilization of materials, and adherence to standard operating procedures, thereby safeguarding researcher safety and maintaining sample integrity.

Antimicrobial resistance 206 testing revealed resistance to Erythromycin (E15 µg) amongst most isolates.
Importantly, participants who did not wash their hands with soap demonstrated a higher prevalence of contamination, underscoring the critical role of soap use in reducing bacterial transfer.
The findings reveal relatively high bacteriological contamination of shared bicycle handlebars, with most of the bicycle handlebars sampled testing positive for at least one bacterial organism.

text.text: This reinforces the notion that shared mobility surfaces are critical points of exposure and require targeted interventions.
The service providers should implement routine cleaning and disinfection protocols, alongside public awareness campaigns on hand hygiene, to reduce contamination risks and safeguard public health.
Among the bacterial species isolated, S. aureus was the most predominant, followed by total coliforms and E. coli.
The predominance of S. aureus on the bicycle handlebars may reflect its common colonization of human skin and nasal passages and its potential transfer through hand contact.
The detection of E. coli and total coliforms, albeit at lower prevalence, is of particular public health concern as they are indicators of faecal contamination (7).

text.text: Shared bicycles are high-touch surfaces frequently used by multiple individuals in succession, which creates an ideal environment for the persistence and spread of bacteriological organisms.

The antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed widespread resistance patterns, with S. aureus resistant to most of the antibiotics tested, coliforms showing consistent resistance to erythromycin, and E. coli exhibiting selective resistance to tetracycline while retaining sensitivity to amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem.
Prior investigations have also reported the prevalence of pathogenic microorganisms on surfaces, such as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (13, 26).

text.text: This finding signifies the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance in community environments, where resistant strains can persist on high-touch surfaces and increase the risk of transmission, which calls for stricter regulation of antibiotic use to curb misuse and integration of sanitation protocols in shared mobility systems to minimize exposure to resistant strains.

Ugandan studies have also documented extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli (ESBL) and antimicrobial-resistant E. coli across human, animal, and environmental compartments, supporting the importance of community and environmental reservoirs in AMR surveillance (30, 31).

text.text: The study found considerable variation in hand hygiene practices among shared bicycle users, with only a minority reporting consistent hand cleaning after trips.
Among those who practiced hygiene, the majority relied on sanitizers, while a smaller proportion used soap and water, typically accessed in lecture rooms or places of residence.
The reported use of sanitizers may reflect convenience; however, this study did not compare the effectiveness of sanitizing with soap-and-water handwashing.
These findings are consistent with broader public health literature, which often documents a disconnect between knowledge of hygiene practices and their implementation in daily routines (29, 30).

text.text: These findings underscore the importance of integrating hygiene promotion into shared mobility systems, including embedding hand hygiene awareness campaigns within university curricula and health clubs to encourage consistent hand hygiene practices among students and staff.

In addition, the study population was drawn from a university community that is relatively closed and more educated compared to the broader users of public transport in Uganda, restricting the generalizability of findings to diverse settings such as taxis and buses.

Another limitation of the study was that only bicycle handlebar samples were collected, while no hand-rinse or hand-swab samples were obtained from participants because the bacteriological contaminants recovered from handlebars might have originated from previous users, not necessarily the one interviewed, or environmental sources.
Despite these limitations, the study offers important data to inform hygiene interventions and antimicrobial resistance surveillance in communal transport environments.

This study demonstrated that shared bicycle handlebars at Makerere University are contaminated with multiple bacterial species, most notably Staphylococcus aureus, total coliforms, and Escherichia coli, showing that these communal surfaces can carry potentially pathogenic organisms.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed widespread resistance, including multidrug-resistant S. aureus, highlighting the relevance of AMR surveillance beyond clinical settings.

Statistical analysis identified an association between contamination levels and hand hygiene practices, with inadequate hand cleaning before and after use of the shared bicycles associated with a higher prevalence of contamination.
These findings signify that both environmental conditions and user behaviors jointly shape microbial persistence and transmission in shared mobility systems.
Consistent with earlier literature on public transport and other high-contact communal surfaces, our results highlight the urgent need for integrated interventions.

The university administration and the bicycle service provider should prioritize routine cleaning/disinfection of handlebars and other high-touch bicycle surfaces, expand access to hand-washing facilities near docking stations, and implement awareness campaigns that emphasize proper hygiene practices.
In addition, surveillance of antimicrobial resistance in community settings should be strengthened to inform antibiotic stewardship and safeguard public health.
